html:
The Latin American republics are the independent states of Mexico, Central America and South America that took the place of Spanish and Portuguese rule from 1810 onward. On the chart they appear as one bar because their borders kept shifting through the 1800s.

Most were born in the wars of independence of 1810 to 1825, led by Simón Bolívar, José de San Martín and others. Brazil took a different road, becoming an empire in 1822, and Haiti had freed itself from France earlier (see Haitian Revolution). The name "Latin America" itself was coined in the 1830s and spread in the 1850s and 1860s.

Early unions broke apart. Gran Colombia split into Venezuela, Colombia and Ecuador, the Federation of Central America into five states, and Mexico lost about half its land to the United States by 1848. Wars between neighbours redrew more borders, and power often fell to strongmen called caudillos.

From about 1870 to 1930 the region grew by exporting raw goods to Europe and the United States: coffee, beef, wheat, rubber, copper, nitrates and oil (see Amazon rubber boom). Millions of Europeans emigrated there (see mass migration to Argentina).

The 20th century brought the Mexican Revolution, growing cities, populist leaders, US interventions, the Cuban Revolution, and military dictatorships in the 1960s to 1980s. Since then nearly all have returned to elected government. Today most people speak Spanish or Portuguese, and the region is home to about 650 million people.
